entries.748b3daf00037d9d77441a04b93873f32c06cf55: <div sID="gen12433" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="107" osisID="Ps.107" sID="Ps.107"/> <div eID="gen12433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12434" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12435" type="x-p"/> The psalmist, having in the two foregoing psalms celebrated the wisdom, power, and goodness of God, in his dealings with his church in particular, here observes some of the instances of his providential care of the children of men in general, especially in their distresses; for he is not only King of saints, but King of nations, not only the God of Israel, but the God of the whole earth, and a common Father to all mankind. Though this may especially refer to Israelites in their personal capacity, yet there were those who pertained not to the commonwealth of Israel and yet were worshippers of the true God; and even those who worshipped images had some knowledge of a supreme "Numen," to whom, when they were in earnest, they looked above all their false gods. And of these, when they prayed in their distresses, God took a particular care, I. The psalmist specifies some of the most common calamities of human life, and shows how God succours those that labour under them, in answer to their prayers. I. Banishment and dispersion, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.2-Ps.107.9">ver. 2-9</reference>. 2. Captivity and imprisonment, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.10-Ps.107.16">ver. 10-16</reference>. 3. Sickness and distemper of body, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.17-Ps.107.22">ver. 17-22</reference>. 4. Danger and distress at sea, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.23-Ps.107.32">ver. 23-32</reference>. These are put for all similar perils, in which those that cry unto God have ever found him a very present help. II. He specifies the varieties and vicissitudes of events concerning nations and families, in all which God's hand is to be eyed by his own people, with joyful acknowledgments of his goodness, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.33-Ps.107.43">ver. 33-43</reference>. When we are in any of these or the like distresses it will be comfortable to sing this psalm, with application; but, if we be not, others are, and have been, of whose deliverances it becomes us to give God the glory, for we are members one of another.
entries.27043b2c1a236ec867eccf930e8bdeeb12cdae86: <div eID="gen12435" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12434" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Exhortation to Celebrate God's Praises.</title> <div sID="gen12436" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> O give thanks unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , for <hi type="italic">he is</hi> good: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">2</hi> Let the redeemed of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> say <hi type="italic">so,</hi> whom he hath redeemed from the hand of the enemy; <hi type="super">3</hi> And gathered them out of the lands, from the east, and from the west, from the north, and from the south. <hi type="super">4</hi> They wandered in the wilderness in a solitary way; they found no city to dwell in. <hi type="super">5</hi> Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted in them. <hi type="super">6</hi> Then they cried unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in their trouble, <hi type="italic">and</hi> he delivered them out of their distresses. <hi type="super">7</hi> And he led them forth by the right way, that they might go to a city of habitation. 8 Oh that <hi type="italic">men</hi> would praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">for</hi> his goodness, and <hi type="italic">for</hi> his wonderful works to the children of men! <hi type="super">9</hi> For he satisfieth the longing soul, and filleth the hungry soul with goodness. <div eID="gen12436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12437" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A general call to all to give thanks to God, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.1">v. 1</reference>. Let all that sing this psalm, or pray over it, set themselves herein to <hi type="italic">give thanks to the Lord;</hi> and those that have not any special matter for praise may furnish themselves with matter enough from God's universal goodness. In the fountain <hi type="italic">he is good;</hi> in the streams <hi type="italic">his mercy endures for ever</hi> and never fails. <div eID="gen12437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12438" type="x-p"/> II. A particular demand hereof from <hi type="italic">the redeemed of the Lord,</hi> which may well be applied spiritually to those that have an interest in the great Redeemer and are saved by him from sin and hell. They have, of all people, most reason to say that God is good, and his mercy everlasting; these are the <hi type="italic">children of God that were scattered abroad,</hi> whom Christ died to <hi type="italic">gather together in one,</hi> out of all lands, <reference osisRef="John.11.52">John xi. 52</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.31">Matt. xxiv. 31</reference>. But it seems here to be meant of a temporal deliverance, wrought for them when in their distress <hi type="italic">they cried unto the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.6">v. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Is any afflicted? Let him pray.</hi> Does any pray? God will certainly hear and help. When troubles become extreme that is man's time to cry; those who but whispered prayer before then cry aloud, and then it is God's time to succour. In the mount he will be seen. 1. They were in an enemy's country, but God wrought out their rescue: <hi type="italic">He redeemed them from the hand of the enemy</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.2">v. 2</reference>), not by <hi type="italic">might or power,</hi> it may be (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.6">Zech. iv. 6</reference>), nor by <hi type="italic">price or reward</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.13">Isa. xlv. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">but by the Spirit of God</hi> working on the spirits of men. 2. They were dispersed as out-casts, but God gathered them out of all the countries whither they were scattered in the cloudy and dark day, that they might again be incorporated, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.3">v. 3</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Deut.30.4">Deut. xxx. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.12">Ezek. xxxiv. 12</reference>. God knows those that are his, and where to find them. 3. They were bewildered, had no road to travel in, no dwelling place to rest in, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.4">v. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">When they were redeemed</hi> out of the <hi type="italic">hand of the enemy, and gathered out of the lands,</hi> they were in danger of perishing in their return home through the dry and barren deserts. <hi type="italic">They wandered in the wilderness,</hi> where there was no trodden path, no company, but <hi type="italic">a solitary way,</hi> no lodging, no conveniences, no accommodations, no inhabited city where they might have quarters or refreshment. But <hi type="italic">God led them forth by the right way</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.7">v. 7</reference>), directed them to an inn, nay, directed them to a home, <hi type="italic">that they might go to a city of habitation,</hi> which was inhabited, nay which them themselves should inhabit. This may refer to poor travellers in general, those particularly whose way lay through the wilds of Arabia, where we may suppose they were often at a loss; and yet many in that distress were wonderfully relieved, so that few perished. Note, We ought to take notice of the good hand of God's providence over us in our journeys, going out and coming in, directing us in our way, and providing for us places both to bait in and rest in. Or (as some think) it has an eye to the wanderings of the children of Israel in the wilderness for forty years; it is said (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.10">Deut. xxxii. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">God led them about,</hi> and yet here <hi type="italic">he led them by the right way.</hi> God's way, though to us it seems about, will appear at last to have been the right way. It is applicable to our condition in this world; we are here as in a wilderness, have here <hi type="italic">no continuing city,</hi> but dwell in tents as strangers and pilgrims. But we are under the guidance of his wise and good providence, and, if we commit ourselves to it, we shall be <hi type="italic">led in the right way to the city that has foundations.</hi> 4. They were ready to perish for hunger (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Their soul even fainted in them.</hi> They were spent with the fatigues of their journey and ready to drop down for want of refreshment. Those that have constant plenty, and are every day fed to the full, know not what a miserable case it is to be <hi type="italic">hungry and thirsty,</hi> and to have no supply. This was sometimes the case of Israel in the wilderness, and perhaps of other poor travellers; but God's providence finds out ways to <hi type="italic">satisfy the longing soul and fill the hungry soul with goodness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.9">v. 9</reference>. Israel's wants were seasonably supplied, and many have been wonderfully relieved when they were ready to perish. The same God that has led us has fed us all our life long unto this day, has fed us with food convenient, has provided food for the soul, <hi type="italic">and filled the hungry soul with goodness. Those that hunger and thirst after righteousness,</hi> after God, the living God, and communion with him, shall be abundantly <hi type="italic">replenished with the goodness of his house,</hi> both in grace and glory. Now for all this those who receive mercy are called upon to return thanks (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Oh that men</hi> (it is meant especially of those men whom God has graciously relieved) <hi type="italic">would praise the Lord for his goodness</hi> to them in particular, <hi type="italic">and for his wonderful works to</hi> others of <hi type="italic">the children of men!</hi> Note, (1.) God's works of mercy are wonderful works, works of wonderful power considering the weakness, and of wonderful grace considering the unworthiness, of those he shows mercy to. (2.) It is expected of those who receive mercy from God that they return praise to him. (3.) We must acknowledge God's goodness to the children of men as well as to the children of God, to others as well as to ourselves.
entries.c1bcd81f4cf1db3cdf4040ba9797115c57f01b19: <div eID="gen12438" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Divine Goodness towards Prisoners.</title> <div sID="gen12439" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Such as sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, <hi type="italic">being</hi> bound in affliction and iron; <hi type="super">11</hi> Because they rebelled against the words of God, and contemned the counsel of the most High: <hi type="super">12</hi> Therefore he brought down their heart with labour; they fell down, and <hi type="italic">there was</hi> none to help. 13 Then they cried unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in their trouble, <hi type="italic">and</hi> he saved them out of their distresses. <hi type="super">14</hi> He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and brake their bands in sunder. <hi type="super">15</hi> Oh that <hi type="italic">men</hi> would praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">for</hi> his goodness, and <hi type="italic">for</hi> his wonderful works to the children of men! <hi type="super">16</hi> For he hath broken the gates of brass, and cut the bars of iron in sunder. <div eID="gen12439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12440" type="x-p"/> We are to take notice of the goodness of God towards prisoners and captives. Observe, 1. A description of this affliction. Prisoners are said to <hi type="italic">sit in darkness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.10">v. 10</reference>), in dark dungeons, close prisons, which intimates that they are desolate and disconsolate; they sit <hi type="italic">in the shadow of death,</hi> which intimates not only great distress and trouble, but great danger. Prisoners are many times appointed to die; they sit despairing to get out, but resolving to make the best of it. They are <hi type="italic">bound in affliction, and</hi> many times <hi type="italic">in iron,</hi> as Joseph. Thus sore a calamity is imprisonment, which should make us prize liberty, and be thankful for it. 2. The cause of this affliction, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.11">v. 11</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">because they rebelled against the words of God.</hi> Wilful sin is rebellion against the words of God; it is a contradiction to his truths and a violation of his laws. <hi type="italic">They contemned the counsel of the Most High,</hi> and thought they neither needed it nor could be the better for it; and those that will not be counselled cannot be helped. Those that despise prophesying, that regard not the admonitions of their own consciences nor the just reproofs of their friends, contemn the counsel of the Most High, and for this they are bound in affliction, both to punish them for and to reclaim them from their rebellions. 3. The design of this affliction, and that is to bring <hi type="italic">down their heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.12">v. 12</reference>), to humble them for sin, to make them low in their own eyes, to cast down every high, proud, aspiring thought. Afflicting providences must be improved as humbling providences; and we not only lose the benefit of them, but thwart God's designs and walk contrary to him in them if our hearts be unhumbled and unbroken, as high and hard as ever under them. Is the estate brought down with labour, the honour sunk? Have those that exalted themselves fallen down, and is there none to help them? Let this bring down the spirit to confess sin, to accept the punishment of it, and humbly to sue for mercy and grace. 4. The duty of this afflicted state, and that is to pray (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then they cried unto the Lord in their trouble,</hi> though before perhaps they had neglected him. Prisoners have time to pray, who, when they were at liberty, could not find time; they see they have need of God's help, though formerly they thought they could do well enough without him. Sense will make men cry when they are in trouble, but grace will direct them to cry unto the Lord, from whom the affliction comes and who alone can remove it. 5. Their deliverance out of the affliction: <hi type="italic">They cried unto the Lord, and he saved them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.13">v. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">He brought them out of darkness into light,</hi> welcome light, and then doubly sweet and pleasant, <hi type="italic">brought them out of the shadow of death</hi> to the comforts of life, and their liberty was to them life from the dead, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.14">v. 14</reference>. Were they <hi type="italic">fettered? He broke their bands asunder.</hi> Were they imprisoned in strong castles? <hi type="italic">He broke the gates of brass</hi> and the <hi type="italic">bars of iron</hi> wherewith those gates were made fast; he did not put back, but <hi type="italic">cut in sunder.</hi> Note, When God will work deliverance the greatest difficulties that lie in the way shall be made nothing of. Gates of brass and bars of iron, as they cannot keep him out from his people (he was with Joseph in the prison), so they cannot keep them in when the time, the set-time, for their enlargement, comes. 6. The return that is required from those whose bands God has loosed (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let them praise the Lord for his goodness,</hi> and take occasion from their own experience of it, and share in it, to bless him for that goodness which the earth is full of, <hi type="italic">the world and those that dwell therein.</hi>
entries.4416ea090569f973e6e3a24013add87c9cd9b2e2: <div eID="gen12440" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Divine Goodness towards the Afflicted.</title> <div sID="gen12441" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Fools because of their transgression, and because of their iniquities, are afflicted. <hi type="super">18</hi> Their soul abhorreth all manner of meat; and they draw near unto the gates of death. <hi type="super">19</hi> Then they cry unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in their trouble, <hi type="italic">and</hi> he saveth them out of their distresses. <hi type="super">20</hi> He sent his word, and healed them, and delivered <hi type="italic">them</hi> from their destructions. <hi type="super">21</hi> Oh that <hi type="italic">men</hi> would praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">for</hi> his goodness, and <hi type="italic">for</hi> his wonderful works to the children of men! <hi type="super">22</hi> And let them sacrifice the sacrifices of thanksgiving, and declare his works with rejoicing. <div eID="gen12441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12442" type="x-p"/> Bodily sickness is another of the calamities of this life which gives us an opportunity of experiencing the goodness of God in recovering us, and of that the psalmist speaks in these verses, where we may observe, <div eID="gen12442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12443" type="x-p"/> I. That we, by our sins, bring sickness upon ourselves and then it is our duty to pray, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.17-Ps.107.18">v. 17-19</reference>. 1. It is the sin of the soul that is the cause of sickness; we bring it upon ourselves both meritoriously and efficiently: <hi type="italic">Fools, because of their transgression, are thus afflicted;</hi> they are thus corrected for the sins they have committed and thus cured of their evil inclinations to sin. If we knew no sin, we should know no sickness; but the transgression of our life, and the iniquity of our heart, make it necessary. Sinners are fools; they wrong themselves, and all against their own interest, not only their spiritual, but their secular interest. They prejudice their bodily health by intemperance and endanger their lives by indulging their appetites. This their way is their folly, and they need the rod of correction to drive out the foolishness that is bound up in their hearts. 2. The weakness of the body is the effect of sickness, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.18">v. 18</reference>. When people are sick <hi type="italic">their soul abhors all manner of meat;</hi> they not only have no desire to eat nor power to digest it, but they nauseate it, and their stomach is turned against it. And here they may read their sin in their punishment: those that doted most on the meat that perishes, when they come to be sick are sick of it, and the dainties they loved are loathed; what they took too much of now they can take nothing of, which commonly follows upon the overcharging of the heart with surfeiting and drunkenness. And when the appetite is gone the life is as good as gone: <hi type="italic">They draw near unto the gates of death;</hi> they are, in their own apprehension and in the apprehension of all about them, at the brink of the grave, as ready to be turned to destruction. 3. Then is a proper time for prayer: <hi type="italic">Then they cry unto the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.19">v. 19</reference>. Is any sick? Let him pray; let him be prayed for. Prayer is a salve for every sore. <div eID="gen12443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12444" type="x-p"/> II. That it is by the power and mercy of God that we are recovered from sickness, and then it is our duty to be thankful. Compare with this <reference osisRef="Job.33.18">Job xxxiii. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.33.28">28</reference>. 1. When those that are sick call upon God he returns them an answer of peace. They cry unto him and he <hi type="italic">saves them out of their distresses</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.19">v. 19</reference>); he removes their griefs and prevents their fears. (1.) He does it easily: <hi type="italic">He sent his word and healed them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.20">v. 20</reference>. This may be applied to the miraculous cures which Christ wrought when he was upon earth, by a word's speaking; he said, <hi type="italic">Be clean, Be whole,</hi> and the work was done. It may also be applied to the spiritual cures which the Spirit of grace works in regeneration; he sends his word, and heals souls, convinces, converts, sanctifies them, and all by the word. In the common instances of recovery from sickness God in his providence does but speak, and it is done. (2.) He does it effectually: <hi type="italic">He delivereth them out of their destructions,</hi> that they shall neither be destroyed nor distressed with the fear of being so. Nothing is too hard for that God to do who kills and makes alive again, brings down to the grave and raises up, who <hi type="italic">turneth man</hi> almost <hi type="italic">to destruction,</hi> and yet saith, <hi type="italic">Return.</hi> 2. When those that have been sick are restored they must return to God an answer of praise (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.21-Ps.107.22">v. 21, 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let all men praise the Lord for his goodness,</hi> and let those, particularly, to whom God has thus granted a new life, spend it in his service; <hi type="italic">let them sacrifice with thanksgiving,</hi> not only bring a thank-offering to the altar, but a thankful heart to God. Thanksgivings are the best thank-offerings, and shall please the Lord better than an ox or bullock. <hi type="italic">And let them declare his works with rejoicing,</hi> to his honour and for the encouragement of others. <hi type="italic">The living, the living, they shall praise him.</hi>
entries.bc6e29ca14d5c65e542fef38034853df9196701e: <div eID="gen12444" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Divine Goodness to Mariners.</title> <div sID="gen12445" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters; <hi type="super">24</hi> These see the works of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and his wonders in the deep. 25 For he commandeth, and raiseth the stormy wind, which lifteth up the waves thereof. <hi type="super">26</hi> They mount up to the heaven, they go down again to the depths: their soul is melted because of trouble. <hi type="super">27</hi> They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits' end. <hi type="super">28</hi> Then they cry unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in their trouble, and he bringeth them out of their distresses. <hi type="super">29</hi> He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still. <hi type="super">30</hi> Then are they glad because they be quiet; so he bringeth them unto their desired haven. <hi type="super">31</hi> Oh that <hi type="italic">men</hi> would praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">for</hi> his goodness, and <hi type="italic">for</hi> his wonderful works to the children of men! <hi type="super">32</hi> Let them exalt him also in the congregation of the people, and praise him in the assembly of the elders. <div eID="gen12445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12446" type="x-p"/> The psalmist here calls upon those to give glory to God who are delivered from dangers at sea. Though the Israelites dealt not much in merchandise, yet their neighbours the Tyrians and Zidonians did, and for them perhaps this part of the psalm was especially calculated. <div eID="gen12446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12447" type="x-p"/> I. Much of the power of God appears at all times in the sea, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.23-Ps.107.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. It appears to those <hi type="italic">that go down to the sea in ships,</hi> as mariners, merchants, fishermen, or passengers, <hi type="italic">that do business in great waters.</hi> And surely none will expose themselves there but those that have business (among all Solomon's pleasant things we do not read of any pleasure-boat he had), but those that go on business, lawful business, may, in faith, put themselves under the divine protection. <hi type="italic">These see the works of the Lord, and his wonders,</hi> which are the more surprising, because most are born and bred upon land, and what passes at sea is new to them. The deep itself is a wonder, its vastness, its saltness, its ebbing and flowing. The great variety of living creatures in the sea is wonderful. Let those that go to sea be led, by all the wonders they observe there, to consider and adore the infinite perfections of that God whose the sea is, for he made it and manages it. <div eID="gen12447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12448" type="x-p"/> II. It especially appears in storms at sea, which are much more terrible than at land. Observe here, 1. How dangerous and dreadful a tempest at sea is. <hi type="italic">Then</hi> wonders begin to appear in the deep, when God <hi type="italic">commands and raises the</hi> strong <hi type="italic">wind,</hi> which <hi type="italic">fulfils his word,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.148.8">Ps. cxlviii. 8</reference>. He raises the winds, as a prince by his commission raises forces. Satan pretends to be the <hi type="italic">prince of the power of the air;</hi> but he is a pretender; the powers of the air are at God's command, not at his. When the wind becomes stormy it <hi type="italic">lifts up the waves</hi> of the sea, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.25">v. 25</reference>. Then the ships are kicked like tennis-balls on the tops of the waves; they seem to <hi type="italic">mount up to the heavens,</hi> and then they couch again, as if they would <hi type="italic">go down to the depths,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.26">v. 26</reference>. A stranger, who had never seen it, would not think it possible for a ship to live at sea, as it will in a storm, and ride it out, but would expect that the next wave would bury it and it would never come up again; and yet God, who taught man discretion to make ships that should so strangely keep above water, does by his special providence preserve them, that they answer the end to admiration. When the ships are thus tossed the <hi type="italic">soul</hi> of the seaman <hi type="italic">melts because of trouble;</hi> and, when the storm is very high, even those that are used to the sea can neither shake off nor dissemble their fears, but <hi type="italic">they reel to and fro,</hi> and tossing makes them giddy, <hi type="italic">and</hi> they <hi type="italic">stagger</hi> and are sick, it may be, <hi type="italic">like a drunken man;</hi> the whole ship's crew are in confusion <hi type="italic">and</hi> quite <hi type="italic">at their wits' end</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.27">v. 27</reference>), not knowing what to do more for their preservation; all their wisdom is swallowed up, and they are ready to give up themselves for gone, <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.5-Jonah.1.11">Jonah i. 5</reference>, &c. 2. How seasonable it is at such a time to pray. Those that go to sea must expect such perils as are here described, and the best preparation they can make for them is to make sure a liberty of access to God by prayer, for <hi type="italic">then they</hi> will <hi type="italic">cry unto the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.28">v. 28</reference>. We have a saying, "Let those that would learn to pray go to sea;" I say, Let those that will go to sea learn to pray, and accustom themselves to pray, that they may come with the more boldness to the throne of grace when they are in trouble. Even heathen mariners, in a storm, <hi type="italic">cried every man to his god;</hi> but those that have the Lord for their God have a present and powerful help in that and every other time of need, so that when they are at their wits' end they are not at their faith's end. 3. How wonderfully God sometimes appears for those that are in distress at sea, in answer to their prayers: <hi type="italic">He brings them out</hi> of the danger; and, (1.) The sea is still: <hi type="italic">He makes the storm a calm,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.29">v. 29</reference>. The winds fall, and only by their soft and gentle murmurs serve to lull the waves asleep again, so that the surface of the sea becomes smooth and smiling. By this Christ proved himself to be more than a man <hi type="italic">that even the winds and the seas obeyed him.</hi> (2.) The seamen are made easy: <hi type="italic">They are glad because they are quiet,</hi> quiet from the noise, quiet from the fear of evil. Quietness after a storm is a very desirable thing, and sensibly pleasant. (3.) The voyage becomes prosperous and successful: <hi type="italic">So he brings them to their desired haven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.30">v. 30</reference>. Thus he carries his people safely through all the storms and tempests that they meet with in their voyage heaven-ward, and lands them, at length, in the desired harbour. 4. How justly it is expected that all those who have had a safe passage over the sea, and especially who have been delivered from remarkable perils at sea, should acknowledge it with thankfulness, to the glory of God. Let them do it privately in their closets and families. Let them <hi type="italic">praise the Lord for his goodness</hi> to themselves and others, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.31">v. 31</reference>. Let them do it publicly (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.32">v. 32</reference>), <hi type="italic">in the congregation of the people and in the assembly of the elders;</hi> there let them erect the memorials of their deliverance, to the honour of God, and for the encouragement of others to trust him.
entries.bd57c290c42785a28fa4df13bc722552a30cb0f5: <div eID="gen12448" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Wonders of Divine Providence.</title> <div sID="gen12449" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">33</hi> He turneth rivers into a wilderness, and the watersprings into dry ground; <hi type="super">34</hi> A fruitful land into barrenness, for the wickedness of them that dwell therein. <hi type="super">35</hi> He turneth the wilderness into a standing water, and dry ground into watersprings. <hi type="super">36</hi> And there he maketh the hungry to dwell, that they may prepare a city for habitation; <hi type="super">37</hi> And sow the fields, and plant vineyards, which may yield fruits of increase. <hi type="super">38</hi> He blesseth them also, so that they are multiplied greatly; and suffereth not their cattle to decrease. 39 Again, they are minished and brought low through oppression, affliction, and sorrow. <hi type="super">40</hi> He poureth contempt upon princes, and causeth them to wander in the wilderness, <hi type="italic">where there is</hi> no way. <hi type="super">41</hi> Yet setteth he the poor on high from affliction, and maketh <hi type="italic">him</hi> families like a flock. 42 The righteous shall see <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and rejoice: and all iniquity shall stop her mouth. <hi type="super">43</hi> Whoso <hi type="italic">is</hi> wise, and will observe these <hi type="italic">things,</hi> even they shall understand the lovingkindness of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen12449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12450" type="x-p"/> The psalmist, having given God the glory of the providential reliefs granted to persons in distress, here gives him the glory of the revolutions of providence, and the surprising changes it sometimes makes in the affairs of the children of men. <div eID="gen12450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12451" type="x-p"/> I. He gives some instances of these revolutions. <div eID="gen12451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12452" type="x-p"/> 1. Fruitful countries are made barren and barren countries are made fruitful. Much of the comfort of this life depends upon the soil in which our lot is cast. Now, (1.) The sin of man has often marred the fruitfulness of the soil and made it unserviceable, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.33-Ps.107.34">v. 33, 34</reference>. Land watered with <hi type="italic">rivers</hi> is sometimes <hi type="italic">turned into a wilderness,</hi> and that which had been full of water-springs now has not so much as water-streams; it is turned <hi type="italic">into dry</hi> and <hi type="italic">sandy ground,</hi> that has not consistency and moisture enough to produce any thing valuable. Many <hi type="italic">a fruitful land</hi> is turned into saltness, not so much from natural causes as from the just judgment of God, who thus punished <hi type="italic">the wickedness of those that dwell therein;</hi> as the vale of Sodom became a salt sea. Note, If the land be bad, it is because the inhabitants are so. Justly is the ground made unfruitful to those that bring not forth fruit unto God, but serve Baal with their corn and wine. (2.) The goodness of God has often mended the barrenness of the soil, and turned a <hi type="italic">wilderness,</hi> a land o drought, <hi type="italic">into water-springs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.35">v. 35</reference>. The land of Canaan, which was once the glory of all lands for fruitfulness, is said to be, at this day, a fruitless, useless, worthless spot of ground, as was foretold, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.23">Deut. xxix. 23</reference>. This land of ours, which formerly was much of it an uncultivated desert, is now full of all good things, and <hi type="italic">more abundant honour</hi> is <hi type="italic">given to that part which lacked.</hi> Let the plantations in America, and the colonies settled there, compared with the desolations of many countries in Asia and Europe, that formerly were famous, expound this. <div eID="gen12452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12453" type="x-p"/> 2. Necessitous families are raised and enriched, while prosperous families are impoverished and go to decay. If we look broad in the world, (1.) We see many greatly increasing whose beginning was small, and whose ancestors were mean and made no figure, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.36-Ps.107.38">v. 36-38</reference>. Those that were <hi type="italic">hungry</hi> are made <hi type="italic">to dwell</hi> in fruitful lands; there they take root, and gain a settlement, and <hi type="italic">prepare a city for habitation</hi> for themselves and theirs after them. Providence puts good land under their hands, and they build upon it. Cities took rise from rising families. But as lands, will not serve for men without lodgings, and therefore they must <hi type="italic">prepare a city of habitation,</hi> so lodgings, though ever so convenient, will not serve without lands, and therefore they must <hi type="italic">sow the fields, and plant vineyards</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.37">v. 37</reference>), for the king himself is served of the field. And yet the fields, though favoured with water-springs, will not <hi type="italic">yield fruits of increase,</hi> unless they be sown, nor will vineyards be had, unless they be planted; man's industry must attend God's blessing, and then God's blessing will crown man's industry. The fruitfulness of the soil should engage, for it does encourage, diligence; and, ordinarily, <hi type="italic">the hand of the diligent,</hi> by the blessing of God, <hi type="italic">makes rich,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.38">v. 38</reference>. <hi type="italic">He blesses them also, so that they are,</hi> in a little time, <hi type="italic">multiplied greatly, and</hi> he <hi type="italic">diminishes not their cattle.</hi> As in the beginning, so still it is, by the blessing of God, that the earth and all the creatures <hi type="italic">increase and multiply</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.22">Gen. i. 22</reference>), and we depend upon God for the increase of the cattle as well as for the increase of the ground. Cattle would decrease many ways if God should permit it, and men would soon suffer by it. (2.) We see many that have thus suddenly risen as suddenly sunk and brought to nothing (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.39">v. 39</reference>): <hi type="italic">Again they are diminished and brought low</hi> by adverse providences, and end their days as low as they began them; or their families after them lose as fast a they got, and scatter what they heaped together. Note, Worldly wealth is an uncertain thing, and often those that are filled with it, ere they are aware, grow so secure and sensual with it that, ere they are aware, they lose it again. Hence it is called <hi type="italic">deceitful riches</hi> and the <hi type="italic">mammon of unrighteousness.</hi> God has many ways of making men poor; he can do it by <hi type="italic">oppression, affliction, and sorrow,</hi> as he tempted Job and brought him low. <div eID="gen12453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12454" type="x-p"/> 3. Those that were high and great in the world are abased, and those that were mean and despicable are advanced to honour, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.40-Ps.107.41">v. 40, 41</reference>. We have seen, (1.) Princes dethroned and reduced to straits. <hi type="italic">He pours contempt upon</hi> them, even among those that have idolized them. Those that exalt themselves God will abase, and, in order thereunto, will infatuate: He makes <hi type="italic">them to wander in the wilderness, where there is no way.</hi> He baffles those counsels by which they thought to support themselves, and their own power and pomp, and drives them headlong, so that they know not what course to steer, nor what measures to take. We met with this before, <reference osisRef="Job.12.24-Job.12.25">Job xii. 24, 25</reference>. (2.) Those of low degree advanced to the posts of honour (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.41">v. 41</reference>): <hi type="italic">Yet setteth he the poor on high,</hi> raiseth <hi type="italic">from the dust</hi> to the <hi type="italic">throne of glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.8">1 Sam. ii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.113.7-Ps.113.8">Ps. cxiii. 7, 8</reference>. Those that were afflicted and trampled on are not only delivered, but set on high out of the reach of their troubles, above their enemies, and have dominion over those to whom they had been in subjection. That which adds to their honour, and strengthens them in their elevation, is the multitude of their children: <hi type="italic">He maketh him families like a flock</hi> of sheep, so numerous, so useful, so sociable with one another, and so meek and peaceable. He that sent them meat sent them mouths. <hi type="italic">Happy is the man that has his quiver filled</hi> with arrows, for he shall boldly <hi type="italic">speak with the enemy in the gate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.127.5">Ps. cxxvii. 5</reference>. God is to be acknowledged both in setting up families and in building them up. Let not princes be envied, nor the poor despised, for God has many ways of changing the condition of both. <div eID="gen12454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12455" type="x-p"/> II. He makes some improvement of these remarks; such surprising turns as these are of use, 1. For the solacing of saints. They observe these dispensations with pleasure (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.42">v. 42</reference>): <hi type="italic">The righteous shall see it and rejoice</hi> in the glorifying of God's attributes and the manifesting of his dominion over the children of men. It is a great comfort to a good man to see how God manages the children of men, as the potter does the clay, so as to serve his own purposes by them, to see despised virtue advanced and impious pride brought low to the dust, to see it evinced beyond dispute that <hi type="italic">verily there is a God that judges in the earth.</hi> 2. For the silencing of sinners: <hi type="italic">All iniquity shall stop her mouth;</hi> it shall be a full conviction of the folly of atheists, and of those that deny the divine providence; and, forasmuch as practical atheism is at the bottom of all sin, it shall in effect <hi type="italic">stop the mouth of all iniquity.</hi> When sinners see how their punishment answers to their sin, and how justly God deals with them in taking away from them those gifts of his which they had abused, they shall not have one word to say for themselves; for God will be justified, he will be clear. 3. For the satisfying of all concerning the divine goodness (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.43">v. 43</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whoso is wise, and will observe these things,</hi> these various dispensations of divine providence, <hi type="italic">even they shall understand the lovingkindness of the Lord.</hi> Here is, (1.) A desirable end proposed, and that is, rightly to <hi type="italic">understand the loving kindness of the Lord.</hi> It is of great use to us, in religion, to be fully assured of God's goodness, to be experimentally acquainted and duly affected with it, that his <hi type="italic">lovingkindness</hi> may be <hi type="italic">before our eyes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.26.3">Ps. xxvi. 3</reference>. (2.) A proper means prescribed for attaining this end, and that is a due observance of God's providence. We must lay up these things, mind them, and keep them in mind, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.19">Luke ii. 19</reference>. (3.) A commendation of the use of this means as an instance of true wisdom: <hi type="italic">Whoso is wise,</hi> let him by this both prove his wisdom and improve it. A prudent observance of the providences of God will contribute very much to the accomplishing of a good Christian.  <chapter eID="Ps.107"/> <div eID="gen12455" type="x-p"/>

entries.32bcbc60b1ac9b23d7f9c079deb0b97de412ec4d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6768"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 107</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.107.1-Ps.107.43">Psa 107:1-43</reference>. Although the general theme of this Psalm may have been suggested by God's special favor to the Israelites in their restoration from captivity, it must be regarded as an instructive celebration of God's praise for His merciful providence to all men in their various emergencies. Of these several are given--captivity and bondage, wanderings by land and sea, and famine; some as evidences of God's displeasure, and all the deliverances as evidence of His goodness and mercy to them who humbly seek Him.</title> <div sID="gen10384" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6768"/>1-2. This call for thankful praise is the burden or chorus (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.107.8">Psa 107:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.15">15</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen10384" type="x-p"/>
entries.14aa6298ce3437b0d4aa572a79dc39a8363c9c09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6770"/><div sID="gen10388" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6770"/><hi type="bold">3. gathered--</hi>alluding to the dispersion of captives throughout the Babylonian empire.<div eID="gen10388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the south--</hi>literally, "the sea," or, Red Sea (<reference osisRef="Ps.114.3">Psa 114:3</reference>), which was on the south. <div eID="gen10389" type="x-p"/>
entries.f06df0b71b857d1c999ab776a5b7388d1bac8430: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6771"/><div sID="gen10390" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6771"/>4-7. A graphic picture is given of the sufferings of those who from distant lands returned to Jerusalem; or,<div eID="gen10390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10391" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">city of habitation--</hi>may mean the land of Palestine. <div eID="gen10391" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8b6e6bfdf86cac25abd1e79ed7827296d0540bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6773"/><div sID="gen10393" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6773"/><hi type="bold">8-9. To the chorus is added, as a reason for praise, an example of the extreme distress from which they had been delivered--</hi>extreme hunger, the severest privation of a journey in the desert. <div eID="gen10393" type="x-p"/>
entries.bdddc511bc1af41166d8c15ec027958d16f00b2f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6774"/><div sID="gen10394" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6774"/><hi type="bold">10-16. Their sufferings were for their rebellion against (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.28">Psa 105:28</reference>) the words, or purposes, or promises, of God for their benefit. When humbled they cry to God, who delivers them from bondage, described as a dark dungeon with doors and bars of metal, in which they are bound in iron--</hi>that is, chains and fetters.<div eID="gen10394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10395" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shadow of death--</hi>darkness with danger (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">Psa 23:4</reference>). <div eID="gen10395" type="x-p"/>
entries.23401cc3204c4f3ae3cc93b2a2ef51e0deeb00ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6776"/><div sID="gen10397" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6776"/>17-22. Whether the same or not, this exigency illustrates that dispensation of God according to which sin brings its own punishment.<div eID="gen10397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10398" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are afflicted--</hi>literally, "afflict themselves," that is, bring on disease, denoted by loathing of food, and drawing <div eID="gen10398" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef1e8f82ac3c2ca57315ea980143211350b84a33: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6779"/><div sID="gen10403" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6779"/>23-32. Here are set forth the perils of seafaring, futility of man's, and efficiency of God's, help.<div eID="gen10403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10404" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go ... sea--</hi>alluding to the elevation of the land at the coast. <div eID="gen10404" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb8294ce6310190f8799c233c165518708693d48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6784"/><div sID="gen10410" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6784"/><hi type="bold">33-41. He turneth rivers into a wilderness, &c.--</hi>God's providence is illustriously displayed in His influence on two great elements of human prosperity, the earth's productiveness and the powers of government. He punishes the wicked by destroying the sources of fertility, or, in mercy, gives fruitfulness to deserts, which become the homes of a busy and successful agricultural population. By a permitted misrule and tyranny, this scene of prosperity is changed to one of adversity. He rules rulers, setting up one and putting down another. <div eID="gen10410" type="x-p"/>
entries.4cccfc555cd4b43473cde228d2f250e9f8ac0801: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6786"/><div sID="gen10412" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6786"/>42-43. In this providential government, good men will rejoice, and the cavils of the wicked will be stopped (<reference osisRef="Job.5.16">Job 5:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.15">Is 52:15</reference>), and all who take right views will appreciate God's unfailing mercy and unbounded love. <chapter eID="Ps.107"/>

entries.65b52625df16d235c49c1170054f4ad494eb9568: <div eID="gen22221" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22222" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22223" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22223" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22222" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22224" type="x-p"/> A thanksgiving of the people for deliverance from difficulties and dangers; their state compared to a journey through a frightful wilderness, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.1-Psa.107.9">Psa 107:1-9</reference>; to confinement in a dreary dungeon, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.10-Psa.107.16">Psa 107:10-16</reference>; to a dangerous malady, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.17-Psa.107.22">Psa 107:17-22</reference>; to a tempest at sea, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.23-Psa.107.32">Psa 107:23-32</reference>. The psalmist calls on men to praise God for the merciful dispensations of his providence, in giving rain and fruitful seasons, after affliction by drought and famine, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.33-Psa.107.38">Psa 107:33-38</reference>; for supporting the poor in affliction, and bringing down the oppressors, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.39-Psa.107.41">Psa 107:39-41</reference>. The use which the righteous should make of these providences, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.42">Psa 107:42</reference>; and the advantage to be derived from a due consideration of God's merciful providence, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.43">Psa 107:43</reference>. <div eID="gen22224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22225" type="x-p"/> This Psalm has no title, either in the Hebrew, or any of the Versions; the word "Hallelujah," which is prefixed to some of the latter, is no title, but was most probably borrowed from the conclusion of the preceding Psalm. The author is unknown; but it was probably like Psalms 105 and 106, made and sung at the dedication of the second temple. The three Psalms seem to be on the same subject. In them the author has comprised the marvellous acts of the Lord towards his people; the transgressions of this people against God; the captivities and miseries they endured in consequence; and finally God's merciful kindness to them in their restoration from captivity, and re-establishment in their own land. <div eID="gen22225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22226" type="x-p"/> This Psalm seems to have been sung in parts: the <reference osisRef="Psa.107.8">Psa 107:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.15">Psa 107:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.21">Psa 107:21</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Psa.107.31">Psa 107:31</reference>, with the <reference osisRef="Psa.107.6">Psa 107:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.13">Psa 107:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.19">Psa 107:19</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Psa.107.28">Psa 107:28</reference>, forming what may be called the burden of the song. In singing of which the whole chorus joined. <div eID="gen22226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22227" type="x-p"/> We may easily perceive that the Psalm must have been sung in alternate parts, having a double burden, or intercalary verse often recurring, and another immediately following, giving a reason for the former. See the <reference osisRef="Psa.107.8">Psa 107:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Psa.107.9">Psa 107:9</reference>, the <reference osisRef="Psa.107.15">Psa 107:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Psa.107.16">Psa 107:16</reference>, the <reference osisRef="Psa.107.21">Psa 107:21</reference> and <reference osisRef="Psa.107.22">Psa 107:22</reference>, the <reference osisRef="Psa.107.31">Psa 107:31</reference> and <reference osisRef="Psa.107.32">Psa 107:32</reference>, and the <reference osisRef="Psa.107.42">Psa 107:42</reference> and <reference osisRef="Psa.107.43">Psa 107:43</reference>, which may be reckoned under the same denomination. Dr. Lowth, in his 29th prelection, has made some excellent remarks on this Psalm. "It is observable," says he, "that after each of the intercalary verses one is added, expressive of deliverance or praise. I would farther observe, that if the Psalm be supposed to be made with a view to the alternate response of one side of the choir to the other, then it may be considered as if it were written exactly after the method of the ancient pastorals, where, be the subject of their verse what it will, each swain endeavors to excel the other; and one may perceive their thoughts and expressions gradually to arise upon each other; and hence a manifest beauty may be discovered in this Divine pastoral. We will suppose, then, that the author composed it for the use of his brethren the Jews, when, in the joy of their hearts, they were assembled after their return from captivity. At such a time, what theme could be so proper for the subject of his poem, as the manifest goodness of Almighty God? The first performers, therefore, invite the whole nation to praise God for this; a great instance of it being their late return from captivity. At <reference osisRef="Psa.107.10">Psa 107:10</reference>, the other side take the subject, and rightly observe that the return of their great men, who were actually in chains, was a more remarkable instance of God's mercy to them, than the return of the people in general, who were only dispersed, we may suppose, up and down the open country. Then the first performers beautitully compare this unexpected deliverance to that which God sometimes vouchsafes to the languishing dying man, when he recalls, as it were, the sentence of death, and restores him to his former vigor. The others again compare it, with still greater strength and expression, to God's delivering the affrighted mariner from all the dreadful horrors of the ungovernable and arbitrary ocean. But the first, still resolved to outdo the rest, recur to that series of wonderful works which God had vouchsafed to their nation, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.32">Psa 107:32</reference>, and of which they had so lately such a convincing proof. Wherefore at last, as in a common chorus, they all conclude with exhorting each other to a serious consideration of these things, and to make a proper return to Almighty God for them. "No doubt the composition of this Psalm is admirable throughout; and the descriptive part of it adds at least its share of beauty to the whole; but what is most to be admired is its conciseness, and withal the expressiveness of the diction, which strikes the imagination with inimitable elegance. The weary and bewildered traveler, the miserable captive in the hideous dungeon, the sick and dying man, the seaman foundering in a storm, are described in so affecting a manner, that they far exceed any thing of the kind, though never so much labored." I may add that had such an Idyl appeared in Theocritus or Virgil, or had it been found as a scene in any of the Greek tragedians, even in Aeschylus himself, it would have been praised up to the heavens, and probably been produced as their master-piece. <div eID="gen22227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22228" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen22228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22229" type="x-p"/> O give thanks - Here is a duty prescribed; and the reasons of it are immediately laid down. <div eID="gen22229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22230" type="x-p"/> 1. He is good. This is his nature. <div eID="gen22230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22231" type="x-p"/> 2. His mercy endureth for ever. <div eID="gen22231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22232" type="x-p"/> This is the stream that flows from the fountain of his goodness.
entries.9cc2e5ed969d816b4b57444b0f9b0353a0f48be7: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen22232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22233" type="x-p"/> Let the redeemed of the Lord say so - For they have had the fullest proof of this goodness, in being saved by the continuing stream of his mercy.
entries.d94f29d535b9a13301d28a49baf7099ede7c15f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen22233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22234" type="x-p"/> And gathered them out of the lands - Though many Jews returned into Jerusalem from various parts of the world, under the reigns of Darius Hystaspes, Artaxerxes, and Alexander the Great; yet this prophecy has its completion only under the Gospel, when all the ends of the earth hear the salvation of God.
entries.091e95abca2b6c2d8d6a3a4d87c0ce9ba4776263: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen22234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22235" type="x-p"/> They wandered in the wilderness - Here begins the Finest comparison: the Israelites in captivity are compared to a traveler in a dreary, uninhabited, and barren desert, spent with hunger and thirst, as well as by the fatigues of the journey, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.5">Psa 107:5</reference>.
entries.1ff2ad532919eb50a02fee4755683346fb9c2275: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen22235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22236" type="x-p"/> Then they cried unto the Lord - When the Israelites began to pray heartily, and the eyes of all the tribes were as the eyes of one man turned unto the Lord, then he delivered them out of their distresses.
entries.de70e8b6ba23cfa0309d43c9842570621e6c7357: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen22236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22237" type="x-p"/> That they might go to a city of habitation - God stirred up the heart of Cyrus to give them liberty to return to their own land: and Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, at different times, brought many of them back to Judea.
entries.4b7574cde8489a10ad04fd97516f36e752e5a1c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen22237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22238" type="x-p"/> O that men would praise the Lord - This is what is called the intercalary verse, or burden of each part of this responsive song: see the introduction. God should be praised because he is good. We naturally speak highly of those who are eminent. God is infinitely excellent, and should be celebrated for his perfections. But he does wonders for the children of men; and, therefore, men should praise the Lord. And he is the more to be praised, because these wonders, נפלאות niphlaoth, miracles of mercy and grace, are done for the undeserving. They are done לבני אדם libney adam, for the children of Adam, the corrupt descendants of a rebel father.
entries.57d9baa35f19089b235b40aa5da46fa9446da52d: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen22238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22239" type="x-p"/> For he satisfieth the longing soul - This is the reason which the psalmist gives for the duty of thankfulness which he prescribes. The longing soul, נפש שוקקה nephesh shokekah, the soul that pushes forward in eager desire after salvation.
entries.cacb0473a44291cc51073df85e2947dd952cf538: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen22239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22240" type="x-p"/> Such as sit in darkness - Here begins the Second similitude, which he uses to illustrate the state of the captives in Babylon viz., that of a prisoner in a dreary dungeon. <div eID="gen22240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22241" type="x-p"/> 1. They sit in or inhabit darkness. They have no light, no peace, no prosperity. <div eID="gen22241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22242" type="x-p"/> 2. "In the shadow of death." The place where death reigns, over which he has projected his shadow; those against whom the sentence of death has been pronounced. <div eID="gen22242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22243" type="x-p"/> 3. They are bound in this darkness, have no liberty to revisit the light, and cannot escape from their executioners. <div eID="gen22243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22244" type="x-p"/> 4. They are afflicted, not only by want and privation in general, but they are tortured in the prison, עני oni, afflicted, humbled, distressed. <div eID="gen22244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22245" type="x-p"/> 5. Their fetters are such as they cannot break; they are iron. The reason of their being in this wretched state is given.
entries.3a0f89c8b60f7c0e0c33ba57987245c62ed1396b: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen22245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22246" type="x-p"/> Because they rebelled against the words of God - <div eID="gen22246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22247" type="x-p"/> 1. God showed them their duty and their interest, and commanded them to obey his word; but they cast off all subjection to his authority, acted as if they were independent of heaven and earth, and broke out into open rebellion against him. <div eID="gen22247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22248" type="x-p"/> 2. He counsealed and exhorted them to return to him: but they contemned his advice, and turned his counsel into ridicule. <div eID="gen22248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22249" type="x-p"/> 3. As lenient means were ineffectual, he visited them in judgment: hence it is added,
entries.ab22344c35cef42d1b3c0ab351aab88319dc90b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen22249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22250" type="x-p"/> He brought down their heart with labor - He delivered them into the hands of their enemies. and, as they would not be under subjection to God, he delivered them into slavery to wicked men: "So they fell down, and there was none to help;" God had forsaken them because they had forsaken him.
entries.478d20f48403255176743f52afdb4e3b28dec45e: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen22250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22251" type="x-p"/> Then they cried unto the Lord in their trouble - This was the salutary effect which their afflictions produced: they began to cry to God for mercy and help; and God mercifully heard their prayer, and reversed their state; for,
entries.99465fef01a804c522112bbc18a4584b7e9ef2c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen22251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22252" type="x-p"/> He brought then out of darkness - <div eID="gen22252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22253" type="x-p"/> 1. Gave them again peace and prosperity. <div eID="gen22253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22254" type="x-p"/> 2. Repealed the sentence of death. <div eID="gen22254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22255" type="x-p"/> 3. "Unbound the poor prisoners." <div eID="gen22255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22256" type="x-p"/> 4. Broke their iron bonds in sunder.
entries.0b35887d130ac523e1bdd2f6ed1381ee6cbe0097: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen22256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22257" type="x-p"/> O that men, etc. - This is the intercalary verse, or burden, of the second part, as it was of the first. See <reference osisRef="Psa.107.8">Psa 107:8</reference>.
entries.27dd114a5c9e3f2337678398307a643d24324650: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen22257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22258" type="x-p"/> For he hath broken - This is the reason given for thanks to God for his deliverance of the captives. It was not a simple deliverance; it was done so as to manifest the irresistible power of God. He tore the prison in pieces, and cut the bars of iron asunder.
entries.d974d8187c780434a138ca73f70e789256140441: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen22258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22259" type="x-p"/> Fools because of their transgression - This is the Third comparison; the captivity being compared to a person in a dangerous malady. Our Version does not express this clause well: Fools מדרך פשעם midderech pisham, because of the way of their transgressions, are afflicted. Most human maladies are the fruits of sin; misery and sin are married together in bonds that can never be broken.
entries.f25a9ad08f851aca18d06fe407e778f345289d14: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen22259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22260" type="x-p"/> Their soul abhorreth all manner of meat - A natural description of a sick man: appetite is gone, and all desire for food fails; nutriment is no longer necessary, for death has seized upon the whole frame. See a similar image, <reference osisRef="Job.33.20">Job 33:20</reference> (note).
entries.15c5d5064f7ae52e98960faea52552a3fe14c92a: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen22260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22261" type="x-p"/> Then they cry - The effect produced by affliction as before.
entries.2058fa7c1f56af973f6bb0f0401b0839abd58d61: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen22261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22262" type="x-p"/> He sent his word, and healed them - He spoke: "Be thou clean, be thou whole;" and immediately the disease departed; and thus they were delivered from the destructions that awaited them.
entries.348d744924620d09edfad2cd68e6581048a10dde: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen22262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22263" type="x-p"/> O that men, etc. - The intercalary verse, or burden, as before.
entries.ce0338c5be4b673f3df12eef9db9db1078a5c2aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen22263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22264" type="x-p"/> And let them sacrifice - For their healing they should bring a sacrifice; and they should offer the life of the innocent animal unto God, as he has spared their lives; and let them thus confess that God has spared then when they deserved to die; and let them declare also "his works with rejoicing;" for who will not rejoice when he is delivered from death?
entries.1a277cc9a43b12e67042855ac2e4e6ef2d7df923: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen22264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22265" type="x-p"/> They that go down to the sea in ships - This is the Fourth comparison. Their captivity was as dangerous and alarming as a dreadful tempest at sea to a weather-beaten mariner.
entries.dc567c8af69cd8f1d017af61f6f3bba4b291d046: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen22265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22266" type="x-p"/> These see the works of the Lord - Splendid, Divinely impressive, and glorious in fine weather. <div eID="gen22266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22267" type="x-p"/> His wonders in the deep - Awfully terrible in a tempest.
entries.9c4d11282ebc64bf4b475fefa2ac3f270e2383ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen22267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22268" type="x-p"/> For he commandeth - And what less than the command of God can raise up such winds as seem to heave old Ocean from his bed?
entries.1d86e6e96795ae8bbca8767e8cb0e0eedfd28154: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen22268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22269" type="x-p"/> They mount up to the heaven - This is a most natural and striking description of the state of a ship at sea in a storm: when the sea appears to run mountains high, and the vessel seems for a moment to stand on the sharp ridge of one most stupendous, with a valley of a frightful depth between it and a similar mountain, which appears to be flying in the midst of heaven, that it may submerge the hapless bark, when she descends into the valley of death below. This is a sight the most terrific that can be imagined: nor can any man conceive or form an adequate idea of it, who has not himself been at sea in such a storm. <div eID="gen22269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22270" type="x-p"/> Their soul is melted because of trouble - This is not less expressive than it is descriptive. The action of raising the vessel to the clouds, and precipitating her into the abyss, seems to dissolve the very soul: the whole mind seems to melt away, so that neither feeling, reflection, nor impression remains, nothing but the apprehension of inevitable destruction! When the ship is buffeted between conflicting waves, which threaten either to tear her asunder or crush her together; when she reels to and fro, and staggers like a drunken man, not being able to hold any certain course; when sails and masts are an incumbrance, and the helm of no use; when all hope of safety is taken away; and when the experienced captain, the skillful pilot, and the hardy sailors, cry out, with a voice more terrible than the cry of fire at midnight, We are All lost! we are all Lost! then, indeed, are they at their wit's end; or, as the inimitable original expresses it, וחל חכמתם תתבלע vechol chochmatham tithballa, "and all their skill is swallowed up," - seems to be gulped down by the frightful abyss into which the ship is about to be precipitated. Then, indeed, can the hand of God alone "bring them out of their distresses." Then, a cry to the Almighty (and in such circumstances it is few that can lift up such a cry) is the only means that can be used to save the perishing wreck! Reader, dost thou ask why I paint thus, and from whose authority I describe? I answer: Not from any books describing storms, tempests, and shipwrecks; not from the relations of shipwrecked marines; not from viewing from the shore a tempest at sea, and seeing a vessel beat to pieces, and all its crew, one excepted, perish. Descriptions of this kind I have read, with the shipwrecked mariner I have conversed, the last scene mentioned above I have witnessed: but none of these could give the fearful impressions, the tremendous and soul-melting apprehensions, described above. "Where then have you had them?" I answer, From the great deep. I have been at sea in the storm, and in the circumstances I describe; and, having cried to the Lord in my trouble, I am spared to describe the storm, and recount the tale of his mercy. None but either a man inspired by God, who, in describing, will show things as they are, or one who has been actually in these circumstances, can tell you with what propriety the psalmist speaks, or utter the thousandth part of the dangers and fearful apprehensions of those concerned in a tempest at sea, where all the winds of heaven seem collected to urge an already crazy vessel among the most tremendous rocks upon a lee shore! God save the reader from such circumstances! <div eID="gen22270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22271" type="x-p"/> When, in the visitation of the winds, He takes the ruffian billows by the top, Curling their monstrous heads, and hanging them, With deafening clamours,on the slippery clouds, That with the hurly death itself awakes! Henry IV. <div eID="gen22271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22272" type="x-p"/> A storm at sea - the lifting the vessel to the clouds - her sinking into the vast marine valleys - the melting of the soul - and being at their wit's end, are well touched by several of the ancient poets. See particularly Virgil's description of the storm that dispersed the fleet of Aeneas, who was himself not unacquainted with the dangers of the sea: - <div eID="gen22272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22273" type="x-p"/> Tollimur in coelum curvato gurgite, et idem <div eID="gen22273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22274" type="x-p"/> Subducta ad manes imos descendimus unda. <div eID="gen22274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22275" type="x-p"/> Aen. iii., 364. <div eID="gen22275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22276" type="x-p"/> Now on a towering arch of waves we rise, <div eID="gen22276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22277" type="x-p"/> Heaved on the bounding billows to the skies. <div eID="gen22277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22278" type="x-p"/> Then, as the roaring surge retreating fell, <div eID="gen22278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22279" type="x-p"/> We shoot down headlong to the gates of hell. <div eID="gen22279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22280" type="x-p"/> Pitt. <div eID="gen22280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22281" type="x-p"/> Rector in incerto est, nec quid fugiatve, petatve, <div eID="gen22281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22282" type="x-p"/> Invenit: ambiguis ars stupet ipsa malis. "The pilot himself is in doubt what danger to shun; or whither to steer for safety he knows not: his skill is nonplussed by the choice of the difficulties before him." <div eID="gen22282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22283" type="x-p"/> See more in the analysis.
entries.b7aa86c4d3e67fe9a2abadf843bb9693d43205f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen22283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22284" type="x-p"/> He maketh the storm a calm - He causes the storm to stand dumb, and hushes the waves. See the original, where sense and sound emphatically meet: - גליהם ויחשו לדממה סארה יקם galleyhem vaiyecheshu lidemamah searah yakem He shall cause the whirlwind to stand dumb, and he shall hush their billows.
entries.f4193cf216cd3c2d36af7b283d35291845d513fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen22284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22285" type="x-p"/> Then are they glad because they be quiet - The turbulence of the sea being hushed, and the waves still, they rejoice to see an end to the tempest; and thus, having fine weather, a smooth sea, and fair wind, they are speedily brought to the desired haven.
entries.5c324899df12a7f75df0e062006dbd7d8a9efc08: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen22285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22286" type="x-p"/> O that men - The intercalary verse, or burden, as before. See <reference osisRef="Psa.107.8">Psa 107:8</reference>.
entries.25d35a8ddcfb4d414920682aeac998c5434c20c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen22286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22287" type="x-p"/> Let them exalt him also in the congregation - Their deliverance from such imminent danger, and in a way which clearly showed the Divine interposition, demands, not only gratitude of heart and the song of praise at the end of the storm, but when they come to shore that they publicly acknowledge it in the congregation of God's people. I have been often pleased, when in sea-port towns, to see and hear notes sent to the minister from pious sailors, returning thanks to the Almighty for preservation from shipwreck, and, in general, from the dangers of the sea; and for bringing them back in safety to their own port. Thus "they exalt the Lord in the congregation, and praise him in the assembly of the elders." And is it not something of this kind that the psalmist requires?
entries.d54284da14b9ced995b268f3708036222bcb5c53: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen22287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22288" type="x-p"/> He turneth rivers into a wilderness - After having, as above, illustrated the state of the Jews in their captivity, and the deliverance which God wrought for them, he now turns to the general conduct of God in reference to the poor and needy; and his gracious Interpositions in their behalf, the providential supply of their wants, and his opposition to their oppressors. On account of the wickedness of men, he sometimes changes a fruitful land into a desert. See the general state of Egypt in the present time: once a fertile land; now an arid, sandy wilderness. Again, by his blessing on honest industry, he has changed deserts into highly fertile ground. And, as for the wickedness of their inhabitants, many lands are cursed and rendered barren; so, when a people acknowledge him in all their ways, he blesses their toil, gives them rain and fruitful seasons, and fills their hearts with joy and gladness.
entries.963b636a1fd9744c4dbe429acb819d65b9eac1e7: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen22288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22289" type="x-p"/> And there he maketh the hungry to dwell - All this seems to apply admirably to the first colonists of any place. They flee from a land of want, an ingrata terra that did not repay their toil, and they seek the wilderness where the land wants only cultivation to make it produce all the necessaries of life. He, by his providence, so guides their steps as to lead them to rivers which they can navigate, and from which they can procure plenty of fish, and shows them wells or springs which they have not digged. The hungry dwell there; and jointly agree, for convenience and defense, to build them a city for habitation. They sow the fields which they have cleared; and plant vineyards, and orchards which yield them in creasing fruits, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.37">Psa 107:37</reference>, and he multiplies their cattle greatly, and does not suffer them to decrease, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.38">Psa 107:38</reference>. What a fine picture is this of the first peopling and planting of America, and of the multiplication and extension of that people; of the Divine blessing on their industry, and the general and astonishing prosperity of their country! May they never again know what is spoken in the following verse:
entries.f3cac6cc5441293db4b92bb2875a8315cd1c8ec7: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen22289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22290" type="x-p"/> Again, they are minished - Sometimes by war, or pestilence, or famine. How minished and brought low was the country already spoken of, by the long and destructive war which began in 1775, and was not ended till 1783! And what desolations, minishings, and ruin have been brought on the fertile empires of Europe by the war which commenced in 1792, and did not end till 1814! And how many millions of lives have been sacrificed in it, and souls sent unprepared into the eternal world! When God makes inquisition for blood, on whose heads will he find the blood of these slaughtered millions? Alas! O, alas!
entries.8c8c1e955e77cf4e74a7a51ef854417c6fc62de4: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen22290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22291" type="x-p"/> He poureth contempt upon princes - How many have lately been raised from nothing, and set upon thrones! And how many have been cast down from thrones, and reduced to nothing! And where are now those mighty troublers of the earth? On both sides they are in general gone to give an account of themselves to God. And what an account! <div eID="gen22291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22292" type="x-p"/> Where there is no way - Who can consider the fate of the late emperor of the French, Napoleon, without seeing the hand of God in his downfall! All the powers of Europe were leagued against him in vain, they were as stubble to his bow. "He came, He saw, and He conquered" almost every where, till God, by a Russian Frost, destroyed his tens of thousands of veteran troops. And afterwards his armies of raw conscripts would have over-matched the world had not a particular providence intervened at Waterloo, when all the skill and valor of his opponents had been nearly reduced to nothing. How terrible art thou, O Lord, in thy judgments! Thou art fearful in praises, doing wonders. <div eID="gen22292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22293" type="x-p"/> The dreary rock of St. Helena, where there was no way, saw a period to the mighty conqueror, who had strode over all the countries of Europe!
entries.ff261d6e955b1d4faf68dc309f646406541f75da: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen22293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22294" type="x-p"/> Yet setteth he the poor on high - This probably refers to the case of the Israelites and their restoration from captivity. But these are incidents which frequently occur, and mark the superintendence of a benign Providence, and the hand of a just God; and are applicable to a multitude of cases.
entries.fb20cb8ef7939cefc8854e0d6cd5e90c516635b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen22294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22295" type="x-p"/> The righteous shall see it - The wicked are as inconsiderate as they are obstinate and headstrong. <div eID="gen22295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22296" type="x-p"/> And rejoice - To have such ample proofs that God ruleth in the earth, and that none that trust in him shall be desolate. <div eID="gen22296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22297" type="x-p"/> All iniquity shall stop her mouth - God's judgments and mercies are so evident, and so distinctly marked, that atheism, infidelity, and irreligion are confounded, and the cause of error and falsehood has become hopeless. It was only the mouth that could do any thing; and that only by lies, calumnies, and blasphemies: but God closes this mouth, pours contempt upon the head and judgment upon the heart. This may also be applied to the case of the Israelttes and the Babylonians. The former, when they turned to God, became righteous; the latter were a personification of all iniquity.
entries.b15bb10fced2410188d3477c74aa7f52ebeed6ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen22297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22298" type="x-p"/> Whoso is wise - That is, He that is wise, he that fears God, and regards the operation of his hand will observe - lay up and keep, these things. He will hide them in his heart, that he sin not against Jehovah. He will encourage himself in the Lord, because he finds that he is a never-failing spring of goodness to the righteous. <div eID="gen22298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22299" type="x-p"/> They shall understand the lovinq-kindness of the Lord - חסדי יהוה chasdey Yehovah, the exuberant goodness of Jehovah. This is his peculiar and most prominent characteristic among men; for "judgment is his strange work." What a wonderful discourse on Divine Providence, and God's management of the world, does this inimitable Psalm contain! The ignorant cannot read it without profit; and by the study of it, the wise man will become yet wiser.  <chapter eID="Ps.107"/> <div eID="gen22299" type="x-p"/>
